confidence_note: The old TR text (a two-group posture experiment measuring cortisol and testosterone, credited to Navarro) is the power-posing study by others (Carney, Cuddy, Yap 2010), whose hormone effects did not replicate; it is NOT in Navarro's book and is dropped. Replaced by Navarro's confidence displays: steepling (he calls it likely the most powerful high-confidence tell), expanding territory when confident (desk items spread out), hands on hips as authority/readiness, hands in pockets with fingers out as low confidence. Source: Throughline Group excerpt, Harper's Bazaar interview. Wording paraphrased.
facts: Navarro says hand steepling may well be the most powerful high-confidence tell.
He says people spread out and take more space when confident.
He suggests arranging desk items so they spread outward rather than piling up.
Hands on hips is a display of authority or readiness.
Hands in pockets with fingers hanging out can show low confidence.
Single signals mislead; confidence reading is also about clusters and baseline.
scene_details: Fingers hanging out of a pocket
tension: Confidence shows in the hands and in the space someone takes before they speak.
opening_idea: Open on the steeple of fingertips.

lessons.idea: Choose the posture you take into a room, since others read it before your words.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A new hire sits tucked in at a table.

reflect_final: Before your next meeting, what do your hands and shoulders usually do in the first minute, and what would you try differently?

use_cases.move: Stand with feet apart and hands visible.
Sit upright and put your hands on the table.

pocket_idea: Hands visible, desk items spread out: confidence shows in the space you take before you speak.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Navarro calls the steeple of fingertips one of the strongest confidence signals.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Navarro: confident people spread out and steeple their fingers; fingers hanging from pockets signal doubt.
